lesson.title: Multiply, Don't Add: Discovering Geometric Sequences
lesson.summary: A geometric sequence multiplies by the same constant ratio from term to term, producing rapid growth or decay that looks very different from the steady pace of an arithmetic sequence.
lesson.body:
In an arithmetic sequence, you get from one term to the next by adding the same constant number every time, the common difference. A geometric sequence changes the operation: you get from one term to the next by multiplying by the same constant number every time, called the common ratio, usually written r. Addition becomes multiplication, and the effect on the sequence is dramatic.

Compare two sequences that start exactly the same way, with the terms 3 and 6:

Arithmetic: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 (add 3 every time)
Geometric: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 (multiply by 2 every time)

For the first two terms, both sequences look identical. By the fifth term, the arithmetic sequence has only reached 15, while the geometric sequence has already reached 48. That gap keeps widening the further you go, because multiplication compounds, each new term carries forward every previous multiplication, while addition only ever adds a flat amount.

To find the common ratio of a geometric sequence, divide any term by the term right before it. For a sequence to be geometric, that division has to give the exact same result no matter which consecutive pair you check, just as an arithmetic sequence needs the exact same difference between every consecutive pair. Check the sequence 3, 6, 12, 24, 48: 6/3 = 2, 12/6 = 2, 24/12 = 2, and 48/24 = 2. Every consecutive pair gives the same ratio, 2, confirming this is a geometric sequence.

This is where exponents come in. Since each term is the previous term multiplied by r, the second term is a_1 times r, the third term is a_1 times r times r, or a_1 times r squared, and so on. In general, the n-th term of a geometric sequence is a_n = a_1 times r raised to the power (n - 1), because you multiply by r exactly n - 1 times to travel from the first term to the n-th term. Check this formula against the sequence above, where a_1 = 3 and r = 2: the fifth term should be a_5 = 3 times 2 to the power 4 = 3 times 16 = 48, which matches the fifth term listed above. The formula also lets you jump ahead without writing out every term in between. The seventh term, for instance, is a_7 = 3 times 2 to the power 6 = 3 times 64 = 192, even though only five terms were ever written out.

The common ratio does not have to be a whole number greater than 1. It can be a fraction between 0 and 1, which produces a shrinking sequence instead of a growing one. Consider 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, where each term is half of the one before it: 50/100 = 0.5, 25/50 = 0.5, 12.5/25 = 0.5, and 6.25/12.5 = 0.5, so r = 0.5. Using the formula with a_1 = 100 and r = 0.5, the fourth term should be a_4 = 100 times 0.5 to the power 3 = 100 times 0.125 = 12.5, which matches. Repeated halving like this shows up often, for example a dose of medicine leaving the bloodstream, or the height a dropped ball reaches on each successive bounce. A common ratio can even be negative, which makes the sequence alternate between positive and negative terms, such as 2, -6, 18, -54, where r = -3.
